newsitem.title: SIERRA LEONE: Nigeria reinforces in Sierra Leone, backing mixed.
newsitem.headline: Nigeria reinforces in Sierra Leone, backing mixed.

text.p: Regional power broker Nigeria has airlifted more troops into Sierra Leone to bolster efforts to end a standoff with coup leaders and their rebel allies and to reinstate civilian President Ahmad Tejan Kabbah.
But its action has prompted a mixed reaction.

Acting in the name of Sierra Leone's West African neighbours, Nigerian gunboats bombarded the capital on Monday but dissident soldiers and rebel allies counter-attacked, forcing its soldiers to give ground in the city.

Some delegates at the Organisation of African Unity summit in Zimbabwe said African leaders resolved during a marathon closed session on Tuesday to isolate the rebel government and support West African efforts to restore democracy.
But at least one West African leader expressed reservations about a military solution to the conflict.
"The agreements between the states of West Africa do not authorise military intervention to restore a regime or organise a counter-coup," Burkina Faso's Blaise Compaore said in Harare.
"This type of operation...could cause further tragedies for the Sierra Leone people," he told Radio France International.
U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan said in Zimbabwe that efforts continued to resolve the stand-off peacefully.
"I hope one would be able to find a way of resolving this situation, for the coup makers to leave and for the legitimate government to go back without much bloodshed," he said.
Nigeria sent at least four helicopters packed with heavily armed soldiers to the capital from Liberia on Tuesday.
General Victor Malu, field commander of the West African ECOMOG force, said Nigeria would also bring in jet bombers as part of efforts to overturn the May 25 coup by junior officers.
Coup leaders have said they are holding 300 captured Nigerian soldiers as human shields against air attacks.
"We agreed a ceasefire...We hope they will respect it because if not, we are building the capacity to carry on the offensive," Malu told Reuters on Tuesday.
Reports from the city said it was calm on Tuesday. Coup leaders put the death toll in the bombardment and fighting at 80. Hospital sources said at least 62 people had been killed.

The United States carried out its largest single-day non-combatant evacuation from the city on Tuesday, bringing out 1,261 foreign and Sierra Leonean civilians by helicopter. The State Department said the airlift was likely to be the last.
Sierra Leone's U.N. ambassador, James Jonah, said he had spoken to Kabbah, who was in Guinea next door to Sierra Leone.
Jonah said ECOMOG was strengthening its positions before beginning a final assault on occupied government headquarters.
"When that is finished, they will go ahead with their objective, which is to remove these thugs who are parading as the government of Sierra Leone," he said.

Sierra Leone, a former British colony racked by civil war since 1991, has suffered three coups in five years. It is one of the world's poorest countries despite a wealth of gem-quality diamonds and other minerals.
The coup leaders have accused Kabbah of failing to consolidate a peace accord signed last November with rebel leader Foday Sankoh, and of encouraging ethnic conflict.
Sankoh, named vice-chairman in Major Johnny Paul Koromah's ruling Armed Forces Revolutionary Council, is being held in Nigeria. He has told his men to back the coup.
Kabbah took office in 1996 after winning multi-party elections which ended four years of military rule.
